newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn government pressured over Nazi pensions.
newsitem.headline: Bonn government pressured over Nazi pensions.

text.p: The German government came under pressure to justify its actions on Friday after it admitted paying convicted Nazi war criminals disability pensions while many of the victims have never received any compensation.

Germany's Jewish leader Ignatz Bubis slammed the payments as a "scandal" that brought the country's legal system into disrepute, and opposition parties called on the government to pass swift new legislation to stop the practice.
Authorities in the city of Bremen said they intended to cancel the pensions of two veterans living abroad after finding out they might be war criminals.

A television network said on Thursday that billions of marks (dollars) were being paid each year, on top of normal pensions, to thousands of Nazi war criminals who suffered a disability linked to World War Two.
A Labour Ministry spokesman confirmed there was no rule to prevent the "victims' pension" being paid even to convicted war criminals, unless they lived outside Germany.
But as a result of the documentary, Bremen said it would apply to the Bonn Labour Ministry to cancel disability pensions paid to two veterans abroad.
One was a former member of a Lithuanian SS battalion now living in the United States, the other a former concentration camp guard in the Baltic region.

Bubis told German Radio it was bad enough that former SS officers and their dependents were receiving extra pensions. But he said he was horrified that there was no special provision to exclude those convicted of war crimes, if they lived in Germany.

"It's depressing when you realise hundreds of Holocaust survivors from the Vilnius and Riga ghettos (in Lithuania and Latvia) were not eligible because they lived in the former Soviet Union, while their (German) guards were," he said.
"This is absolutely scandalous," he added. "This sort of thing brings our legal system into disrepute."
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens joined forces to call on the government to examine the possibility of withdrawing these special "victims' pensions".
The Greens have asked the government to reveal just how many convicted war criminals are receiving disability pensions and to redress the imbalance by fully compensating their victims.
"The payment of billions from taxpayers' money to Nazi criminals and other war criminals is a deep humiliation for Holocaust victims," said Otto Schily, the SPD's deputy leader in parliament.
"The perpetrators are doing better than the victims."

The NDR television documentary said on Thursday that about 50,000 war criminals and members of army units that took part in atrocities were receiving war disability pensions ranging from several hundred to several thousand marks each month.
A Bonn spokesman said there were no legal means for the Labour Ministry to stop payments to the war criminals who lived in Germany. He said he did not know how much they received.
"After a long and controversial debate, the German parliament decided in 1950 that all Germans injured in the war had a right to compensation," he told a news conference.

"Lawmakers made no exception in the law. There was discussion whether Nazi war criminals or human rights violators should be excluded. But they agreed it was the task of the justice authorities to deal with war criminals," he said.
On Thursday, parliament gave a first reading to a Greens bill aimed at ensuring 13,000 Jewish Holocaust survivors in east Europe get the same benefits as counterparts in the West.
They said these victims were currently entitled to a maximum of 1,000 marks ($600) in one-off payments each, while those in Germany received 500 marks ($300) a month.
